title: Displaced Civilians Sifting for Gold in Sudan Killed in Bloody Drone Strike

AD-DAMAZIN, Sudan--On the morning of October 9, Ahmed Ragab Abu Shina, 39,
joined dozens of other displaced people digging for gold in a seasonal
riverbed, known locally as a _khor_ , near the Abu Shandi shelter in Sudan's
Blue Nile State.

At around 9 a.m., a drone flew overhead from the south. No one knew whose it
was, and no one thought it had come for them. Suddenly, an explosive shell
landed in the middle of the _khor_ , where men, women and children were
working side by side.

"After the shell fell, dozens went down, and whoever could flee fled," Ragab
told Drop Site News. "In those moments, no one knew where their family members
or relatives were."

The strike killed 32 displaced people--26 women, four children and two elderly
people--and wounded 43 others, according to Dr. Mustafa Jabrallah, Blue Nile
State's acting health minister.

Jabrallah blamed the drone strike on the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a
powerful paramilitary group that has been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces
(SAF) since April 2023, engulfing the country in what the United Nations
[calls](https://www.emro.who.int/media/news/sudan-1000-days-of-war-deepen-the-
worlds-worst-health-and-humanitarian-crisis.html) "the world's worst health
and humanitarian crisis."

The strike on the _khor_ in the Blue Nile State, in southeastern Sudan, is far
from the RSF's strongholds of Darfur and Kordofan, but it has become an active
front of the war. Though the SAF holds the key administrative centers of the
region, including the state capital, Ad-Damazin, that control is being
challenged by the RSF and its allied rebel group, Sudan People's Liberation
Movement-North (SPLM-N). A recent RSF and SPLM-N attack on al-Hijra, a
neighborhood north of Ad-Damazin, killed four women and wounded 13 others,
Jabrallah said. Elsewhere, RSF and SPLM-N fighters have seized southeastern
border areas like Geissan and Kurmuk. And the SPLM-N has long held or
contested other pockets of the region.

In recent months, the two sides have been fighting over strategic towns and
bases in southeastern Sudan, near the Ethiopian border, according to the[
UN](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168567), and sustained attacks have
displaced thousands of people. The RSF has also pushed further into army-held
territory.

The killing of 32 civilians at the Abu Shandi shelter last week was
particularly devastating. In a
[briefing](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168567) that same day, UN
spokesperson Stephane Dujarric condemned the "horrifying reports" of that
attack and others on civilians, and called for those responsible to be held
accountable.

In attacking the Abu Shandi camp, the Sudan Doctors Network
[said](https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19x2Uwu41f/), the RSF committed "yet
another crime in the ongoing pattern of violations against civilians in
Sudan."

"Targeting gatherings of displaced persons with drones constitutes a war crime
and a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law," the organization
added.

A coalition of RSF and allied forces, the Sudan Founding Alliance,
[denied](https://www.facebook.com/tasis.SFA/posts/pfbid02447niSxRftQLdBnNMTDYfAd4Q2SmALVq7494QPMacwmPNkF4VCdmiy1LVezu957Hl)
carrying out the attack. In a statement on Facebook, a spokesperson said that
blaming the RSF for the strike amounted to making "fabricated and booby-
trapped statements."

## **Violence Chasing the Displaced**

Like many others in the Abu Shandi camp, Ahmed Ragab fled Agro, an area in
Geissan locality about 30 kilometers (19 miles) north of the town of Geissan
and 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of Ad-Damazin, along with people displaced
from Bakori, Geissan, Khor al-Dahab, and al-Jabalain to escape the RSF's
advance. They had lived in safety and peace until what he called "the cursed
war" reached them.

Abu Shandi was supposed to be safe, but once they arrived they struggled to
find food. So they turned to a _khor_ near the shelter and began mining for
gold in the traditional way, rinsing mud with water to recover grains of gold
that they could sell to feed their families.

Buthaina Mohamed Teel Amer, 35, who is also from Agro, fled to Abu Shandi in
August after fighting escalated when the RSF entered Kurmuk, a border town
near Ad-Damazin.

Local aid workers gave plastic sheeting to the displaced people, so that they
could build makeshift shelters, she said. They also handed out rations of a
whole grain called sorghum--each ration weighed only about two kilograms. It
was not enough to eat, so most of the displaced went to work in mining at the
nearby riverbed to earn money for food.

On the day of the strike, Amer was in the _khor_ with members of her family
when the drone dropped a shell into the crowd. Some of the surviving victims
were burned so badly that their relatives could not recognize them and had to
ask for their names to identify them. About 30 people died on the spot, she
said.

"Everyone was screaming," Amer recalled. "As I searched for the wounded, I
found human remains in the trees and in the water of the _khor_. Some of the
injured lay in their own blood, crying out in pain."

Residents of Abu Shandi rushed to the site when they heard the blast, helping
rescue the wounded and bury the dead. No government officials or emergency
workers were present, Ragab said. Civilians handled the rescue themselves.

## **A War in Its Fourth Year**

In April 2023, four years after a popular uprising ousted longtime president
Omar al-Bashir, fighting erupted across Sudan, when a power struggle escalated
into open war between the SAF, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the
RSF, commanded by General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.

At least 150,000 people have died since the war began, but some
[estimates](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/sudan-crisis-situation-
analysis-period-270426-030526) are far higher. About 14 million people have
been driven from their homes, including more than 4.5 million who have fled to
neighboring countries--the single largest displacement crisis in the world.
For those who have remained, starvation is acute. "More people are living in
famine conditions in Sudan than the rest of the world combined,"
[according](https://www.rescue.org/uk/article/crisis-sudan-what-happening-and-
how-help) to the International Rescue Committee.

In Blue Nile, the fighting is pushing people out again, locals told Drop Site
News.

The RSF recently destroyed the main water source in Area 6 of Wad Al-Mahi,
said Mahjoub al-Sheikh Al-Khalifa, commissioner of the locality, and its
fighters stormed the al-Kadalo administrative unit, driving more than 8,000
people toward Roseires, a town north of Ad-Damazin. On October 11, Al-Khalifa
said, the RSF struck and destroyed Um Darfa hospital in the locality.

Drones are now a central weapon for both sides, with strikes killing more than
1,100 people in the first five months of the year, according to UN figures.

Some of the heaviest attacks have come in fiercely contested areas like El-
Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan. The SAF maintains control of the city
while RSF forces have seized areas to the north, west and south. Over the span
of just one week, between September 25 and October 1, RSF drones hit El-Obeid
at least five times, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data
(ACLED) project. "Targets included a shelter at the Land Port, an events hall,
the Sports City complex and Sheikan Dormitory. SAF air defenses intercepted
drones on two of the days," ACLED said in a statement.

The strike on Sheikhan dormitory in Kordofan University, on September 30, was
a double-tap suicide drone attack which killed five people, including two
women and a child, and wounded 26, according to local emergency responders,
who blamed the RSF.

## **Aid Under Fire**

In Abu Shandi, the wounded were carried on donkey carts, farm tractors, and
stretchers to Area 6 of Wad Al-Mahi locality, Ragab said, before the most
critical cases were moved to Ad-Damazin Teaching Hospital.

The condition of the wounded has improved now that medicine is available, he
added, but families are forced to buy whatever the hospital or local aid
groups do not provide for free. A bill for antibiotics, painkillers, and gauze
in private pharmacies can reach 290,000 Sudanese pounds (around $35).

The government has so far offered them nothing, Amer said. At a public
hospital with her 13-year-old daughter, Halima, who was wounded in the strike,
she saw patients contending with swarms of mosquitoes that can carry dangerous
diseases, she said. The government had not supplied the hospital with any
protective nets.

The strike on the Abu Shandi shelter is part of a pattern of RSF attacks on
civilians, Dr. Mohamed Faisal of the Sudan Doctors Network said. Its forces
have systematically targeted shelters, displacement camps, aid convoys,
hospitals and service centers.

"Drone strikes on civilian sites have become a constant of the war," he said.
The RSF attacked a [kindergarten](https://sudantribune.com/article/307774) in
South Kordofan state in December 2025, and a
[shelter](https://www.geeska.com/en/deadly-strikes-el-fasher-shelter-kill-
dozens) in El Fasher two months earlier. These attacks have severely disrupted
relief efforts for the displaced and now threaten the lives of humanitarian
workers. "Several organizations have lost staff, and recent attacks on trucks
carrying aid and on Red Crescent
[workers](https://www.ifrc.org/statement/ifrc-five-sudanese-red-crescent-
volunteers-killed-we-are-horrified) show the dangers they face," he said.

Conditions in the shelters and camps are dire, he added. They lack basic
services like food and medicine, and epidemics and diseases are spreading.

"We don't have accurate statistics, but we have no doubt that these epidemics
and diseases, under the current conditions, will claim more lives," he said.

Al-Khalifa, the commissioner of Wad Al-Mahi, called on the international
community to condemn the RSF's attacks, and asked for an independent,
transparent investigation to identify those responsible for killing women and
children in displacement shelters.

For Amer, the losses are counted in families. "Several girls were killed
alongside their mothers," she said. "An entire family of eight was wiped out
in the strike."
